description: Blacks in CyberSecurity Village promotes diversity, equity, and inclusion in information security, addressing activist OPSEC, infrastructure ownership, and systemic bias in tech.

talks.title: The OPSEC of Protesting: Activist Privacy & Digital Security
talks.teaser: Ochaun Marshall outlines operational security (OPSEC) for civil rights activists, analyzing mobile surveillance threats, burner devices, and encrypted communications.
talks.summary:
The Surveillance Landscape Facing Modern Activists

Civil rights demonstrations and public protests face pervasive surveillance—ranging from automated license plate readers and facial recognition to cell-site simulators (IMSI catchers).

Threat Modeling for Public Demonstrations

Ochaun Marshall establishes practical threat models for organizers, participants, and support personnel before, during, and after public actions.

Practical OPSEC and Device Hardening

Marshall provides actionable digital hygiene practices—including disabling biometrics, utilizing Signal with disappearing messages, and managing location telemetry.

Incident Response and Legal Support Preparedness

The author details emergency device wipe protocols, legal contact preparations, and community support coordination.

talks.title: The Action Plan for Cyber Diversity
talks.teaser: Keith Chapman presents an inside perspective and actionable plan to increase diversity, equity, and inclusion across the information security workforce.
talks.summary:
Keith Chapman delivers a pragmatic, solutions-oriented address at the Blacks in Cybersecurity Village, presenting actionable strategies to expand diversity, equity, and inclusion across the information security industry.

[04:45] Chapman analyzes current demographic representation in corporate cybersecurity teams, highlighting the stark contrast between general population demographics and minority participation in technical and leadership roles. He reflects on his own career trajectory, identifying systemic barriers that impede underrepresented individuals from entering the field, including gatekeeping job requirements, lack of relatable role models, and isolation within homogenous engineering cultures.

[10:11] The talk outlines an actionable roadmap for individuals, community organizations, and corporate leaders. Chapman details practical steps for aspiring professionals seeking non-traditional pathways into cybersecurity, emphasizing continuous self-directed learning, capture-the-flag competitions, and active participation in community meetups. He concludes with recommendations for industry organizations [15:19], urging conference organizers, hiring managers, and senior practitioners to sponsor underrepresented talent, reform interview practices, and build active mentorship networks to strengthen collective defense capabilities through cognitive and cultural diversity.

talks.title: 40 Cores and A CPU: Infrastructure Ownership & Community Empowerment
talks.teaser: Nico Smith emphasizes the importance of Black technologists owning physical and cloud server infrastructure to deliver sovereign services to the community.
talks.summary:
The Imperative of Infrastructure Ownership

True technological independence requires moving beyond consumer-level platform usage toward owning, configuring, and operating sovereign server and network infrastructure.

Building and Managing Independent Compute Capacity

Nico Smith shares real-world experiences deploying bare-metal servers, hypervisors, and distributed storage clusters to serve grassroots community initiatives.

Overcoming Economic and Technical Barriers

Smith addresses the financial, operational, and maintenance challenges inherent in maintaining high-availability community infrastructure.

Fostering Generational Technical Expertise

The author calls for mentorship, hands-on homelabs, and community-driven knowledge sharing to build long-term institutional resilience.

talks.title: Tackling The Remnants of Systematic Discrimination in Tech
talks.teaser: Maurice Turner explores systemic discrimination in the tech industry, analyzing exclusionary language, hiring biases, and structural institutional reforms.
talks.summary:
Uncovering Systemic Inequities in the Technology Sector

The tech industry often perpetuates legacy structural biases through exclusionary culture, unexamined hiring pipelines, and algorithmic discrimination.

The Impact of Discriminatory Language in Technical Lexicons

Maurice Turner examines how legacy terminology (such as master/slave and blacklist/whitelist) reinforces psychological barriers and exclusionary environments.

Structural Barriers to Career Advancement

Turner analyzes empirical data on retention rates, promotion disparities, and venture capital funding gaps affecting underrepresented technologists.

Actionable Institutional and Policy Reforms

The presentation outlines systemic policy changes, inclusive terminology adoption, and measurable accountability frameworks for tech organizations.
